name: Sphagnum moss
habitat: Bogs, fens, wet acidic ground, the wet margins of conifer forest. It forms deep spongy hummocks.
identify: Pale green to rust-red, forming dense soft carpets or hummocks in wet ground.
Each shoot has a tight head of branches at the top like a tiny star or mop.
Holds a startling amount of water — a handful squeezes out like a sponge, and rebounds.
The ground it grows on is acidic and usually squelching.

lookalikes.name: Other mosses
lookalikes.danger: Low — but other mosses lack the absorbency and the acidity that make sphagnum useful, so a substitute performs much worse than expected.
lookalikes.tell: Sphagnum is exceptionally absorbent and grows in standing-wet acidic ground; feather mosses and cushion mosses in drier woodland do not squeeze out water the same way.

preparations.method: Gather clean living moss away from animal traffic, squeeze out the water, boil or steam it if you have fuel, and dry it. Pack it into a cloth pouch or wrap it in clean fabric before it touches the wound.
preparations.for_use: An absorbent wound dressing — it takes up several times its weight in fluid and its acidity discourages bacterial growth. Used at scale for exactly this in the First World War.

cautions: It is NOT sterile. Sporotrichosis ('rose gardener's disease') and other fungal infections are associated with sphagnum handling; boil or dry it if you can, and use it inside a cloth barrier rather than packed raw into tissue.
Never take it from ground fouled by livestock or from a stagnant pool downstream of anything.
It is an absorbent, not an antibiotic. It buys cleanliness, not treatment.
Peat bogs are slow-growing and often protected; take sparingly.
evidence: Historically documented at industrial scale as a surgical dressing; the absorbency and low pH are measurable. Modern clinical use is essentially nil.
